p1.title: Part 1 · Solid-State Materials and Intrinsic Carriers
p1.intro: Electronic materials fall into three categories based on their resistivity (ρ). The resistivity of a semiconductor can be controlled by adding impurity atoms to the crystal.
p1.li1: Elemental semiconductors are formed from a single type of atom in column IV of the periodic table; compound semiconductors combine elements from columns III and V or II and VI.
p1.li2: Germanium was used in many early devices. Silicon replaced it thanks to its higher bandgap, lower cost and the ease of growing an insulating SiO<sub>2</sub> layer.
p1.li3: A Si atom has 4 electrons in its outer shell. Each atom forms covalent bonds with its 4 nearest neighbors, creating a regular diamond lattice. Single crystal material is the most useful for electronics.
p1.li4: At 0 K all bonds are complete and Si behaves as an insulator. As temperature rises, some bonds break and electron-hole pairs are generated.
p1.niText: E<sub>G</sub>: bandgap energy (eV), k = 8.62×10<sup>-5</sup> eV/K, T: absolute temperature (K), B = 1.08×10<sup>31</sup> K<sup>-3</sup>cm<sup>-6</sup> (Si). At room temperature n<sub>i</sub> ≈ 10<sup>10</sup> cm<sup>-3</sup> for silicon.
p1.li5: An electron leaving a bond leaves behind a vacancy with charge +q, called a hole. Hole density is written as p.
p1.li6: For intrinsic silicon n = ni = p. In thermal equilibrium, pn = ni2.
p1.driftText: For intrinsic Si, μ<sub>n</sub> = 1350 and μ<sub>p</sub> = 500 cm<sup>2</sup>/V·s. Hole mobility is lower because hole current involves multiple covalent bond disruptions. Example: at room temperature intrinsic Si has conductivity σ = 2.96×10<sup>-6</sup> (Ω·cm)<sup>-1</sup> and resistivity ρ = 3.38×10<sup>5</sup> Ω·cm, so intrinsic silicon is a poor insulator.

p2.title: Part 2 · Doping, Drift and Diffusion
p2.intro: Doping is adding very small, well-controlled amounts of impurities to a semiconductor. For silicon, impurities come from columns III and V.
p2.donorText: Column V atoms such as phosphorus, arsenic and antimony. With five outer electrons, the atom brings one extra electron that needs very little energy to become free. The ionized donor atom has a fixed charge of +q.
p2.acceptorText: Column III atoms such as boron. An incomplete bond, i.e. a hole, is created. A nearby electron easily moves into the vacancy and the hole travels like a particle. The ionized acceptor has a fixed charge of −q.
p2.f1: Charge neutrality: q(N<sub>D</sub> + p − N<sub>A</sub> − n) = 0    pn = n<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>
p2.li1: At practical doping levels (10<sup>14</sup> ≤ |N<sub>A</sub>−N<sub>D</sub>| ≤ 10<sup>21</sup> cm<sup>-3</sup>) we can take n ≈ N<sub>D</sub>−N<sub>A</sub> or p ≈ N<sub>A</sub>−N<sub>D</sub>.
p2.li2: Majority carrier concentration is set during manufacturing and is independent of temperature. Minority carriers are proportional to ni2 and are therefore strongly temperature dependent.
p2.li3: Doping degrades mobility: impurity atoms scatter the carriers. As total doping N<sub>T</sub> = N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>D</sub> increases, mobility drops rapidly.
p2.diffText: Carriers move from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration, just like a gas spreading across a room.
p2.f2: Einstein relation: D<sub>n</sub>/μ<sub>n</sub> = D<sub>p</sub>/μ<sub>p</sub> = kT/q = V<sub>T</sub> ≈ 25 mV (thermal voltage)

p3.title: Part 3 · Energy Band Model
p3.li1: The conduction band and valence band are the allowed energy states for electrons.
p3.li2: EV: top edge of the valence band. EC: bottom edge of the conduction band. The difference is the bandgap EG.
p3.li3: At 0 K all electrons are in the valence band and no conduction occurs. At T > 0 K thermal energy breaks bonds, electrons move up to the conduction band and holes appear in the valence band.
p3.li4: The donor level ED is very close to EC (about 0.045 eV for phosphorus).
p3.li5: The acceptor level EA is very close to EV (about 0.044 eV for boron).
p3.li6: A compensated semiconductor contains both n-type and p-type dopants. If ND > NA, donor electrons fill the acceptor sites and the remaining ND−NA electrons can move up to the conduction band.
